newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Sons Gwalia eyes mine closures.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sons Gwalia eyes mine closures.

text.p: Australian gold miner Sons of Gwalia Ltd signalled on Friday it would no longer tolerate underperforming properties and would close at least three mines by early next year and review others.

The company's Golden Pig and Frasers underground mines at the Southern Cross deposit will close immediately, while the Copperhead mine at Bullfinch is to close in about six or seven months, Gwalia executive chairman and managing director Peter Lalor told Reuters.
"The whole thrust of mining is changing out there," he said.
With average cash costs around A$444 an ounce, most gold mines in Australia are struggling, Lalor said.
Gold in the spot market fetches around A$450 an ounce.

Gwalia earlier on Friday reported an abnormal loss of A$167.78 million for the year to June 30, due to a write down in the carrying value of operating mining assets and exploration, contributing to an overall net loss of A$128.38 million.
Lalor also said a decision on the Sons of Gwalia underground mine was due in three months.
At its Laverton mine, which is forecast to yield about 50,000 ounces of gold in 1997/98, costs need to come down or it will be placed on care and maintenance, Lalor said.
Lalor said the writedowns reflected reviews of all its mining assets based on an average gold price of A$450 an ounce coupled with non-operating assets.

He said the writedowns were in line with negative changes that had ocurred in the industry such as a decline in the Australian Stock Exchange's gold index, Australian dollar-denominated gold prices and forward premium prices available to miners.
"It's a whole new world out there," Lalor said.
Gwalia will spend about A$28 million on exploration in the current year, 20 percent up on last year, Lalor said.
The funds will be spread around Australia, where the most potential exists for the company to expand, he said.
He said there were parts of Australia that remained under- explored and that offshore opportunities came with extra risks.
"In the wake of the Busang scandal in Indonesia and the problems being experienced in places like the Philippines, " there has to be some cause for concern in those areas," he said.

He also dismissed in part as "broker talk" speculation that the falls in the gold price and subsequent share value of some Australian miners meant North American predator companies would increasingly look to acquire Australian gold producers.
"For the most part, Australian gold producers will not take overseas scrip, which means the North American company must pay cash, which is a big thing to ask," Lalor said.
Australian miners would also be looking for a 20 to 30 percent premium on their pre-bid share price, Lalor added.
